No, research suggests that normally sighted, visually impaired, and blind pedestrians may not always be accurate and reliable at making street crossing decisions. 

Normally sighted pedestrians can be distracted or misjudge the speed and distance of oncoming vehicles. Visually impaired pedestrians may have difficulty detecting and interpreting visual cues, such as traffic signals and pedestrian signals, and may rely on auditory cues, which can be unreliable. Blind pedestrians often rely on auditory cues, such as the sound of traffic, and may use assistive devices like white canes or guide dogs to navigate intersections, but they can still be uncertain about when it is safe to cross.

Studies have shown that all three groups can make errors in judging gaps in traffic, detecting traffic signals, and responding to unexpected events, such as a vehicle running a red light. Therefore, it is essential to provide accessible and reliable cues, such as audible pedestrian signals, tactile markings, and clear signage, to assist all pedestrians, regardless of their visual ability, in making safe and informed street crossing decisions.
